e-4327.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Their Components
e-4327.problem: Find the angle between $\mathbf{a}=\langle 2,-1,1 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle 1,5,-2 \rangle$. Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
e-4327.worked_solution:
Rearranging the dot product formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 5+1\cdot (-2)}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{5}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-5}{\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{30}} \\  & =\frac{-5}{\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta = \arccos \left( -\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{6} \right) \approx 111.9^\circ.
$$

e-4328.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Three Points
e-4328.problem: Find $\angle BAC$ given the points $A(2,-1,-5)$, $B(-1,0,-4)$, and $C(5,1,1).$ Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
e-4328.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A$, $B$, $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨2,-1,-5⟩,\,b=⟨-1,0,-4⟩,\,c=⟨5,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $\triangle ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $\angle BAC = \theta.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13964292/assets/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨-1,0,-4⟩-⟨2,-1,-5⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,1,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨5,1,1⟩-⟨2,-1,-5⟩ \\  & =⟨3,2,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{-3\cdot 3+1\cdot 2+1\cdot 6}{\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-1}{\sqrt{11}\sqrt{49}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{7\sqrt{11}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta = \arccos \left( -\dfrac{1}{7\sqrt{11}} \right) \approx 92.5^\circ.
$$

e-5112.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given the Value of Their Dot Product
e-5112.problem: Given that $\mathbf{a}\cdot \mathbf{b}=-4$, find the angle between $\mathbf{a}=\langle t, \, -2 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle 6, \, t \rangle$. Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
e-5112.worked_solution:
First, since $\mathbf{a}\cdot \mathbf{b}=-4$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =-4 \\ t\cdot 6+(-2)\cdot t & =-4 \\ 6t-2t & =-4 \\ 4t & =-4 \\ t & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨-1,-2⟩,\,b=⟨6,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}\cdot \sqrt{37}} \\  & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{185}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta = \arccos \left( -\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{185}} \right) \approx 107.1^\circ.
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find the angle between $a=⟨4,-3,2⟩$ and $b=⟨3,4,1⟩.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
after.worked_solution:
Rearranging the dot product formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3+(-3)\cdot 4+2\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}\cdot \sqrt{26}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{754}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{2}{\sqrt{754}})≈{85.82}^{∘}.
$$

Note that the position vectors of the points $P,$ $Q$ and $R$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}p=⟨2,4,1⟩,\,q=⟨3,4,2⟩,\,r=⟨3,3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△PQR$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠QPR=\theta .$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13964292/assets/3003f0cb329a8f8ef9bc315c70df4773ac1f0c54843dea1208c68bd0f6227bd1.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =q-p \\  & =⟨3,4,2⟩-⟨2,4,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{PR} & =r-p \\  & =⟨3,3,1⟩-⟨2,4,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot \overset{\to }{PR}}{|\overset{\to }{PQ}||\overset{\to }{PR}|} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 1+0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})={60}^{∘}.
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Find $∠BAC$ given the points $A(2,-1,1)$, $B(3,1,-2)$, and $C(-1,1,1).$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
after.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A$, $B$, $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨2,-1,1⟩,\,b=⟨3,1,-2⟩,\,c=⟨-1,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠BAC=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13964292/assets/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨3,1,-2⟩-⟨2,-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2,-3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨-1,1,1⟩-⟨2,-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,2,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (-3)+2\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}\cdot \sqrt{13}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{182}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{182}})≈{86}^{∘}.
$$

content.problem: Find $∠BAC$ given the points $A(2,1,-1)$, $B(3,-2,2)$, and $C(-1,-2,1).$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
content.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A$, $B$, $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨2,1,-1⟩,\,b=⟨3,-2,2⟩,\,c=⟨-1,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠BAC=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13964292/assets/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨3,-2,2⟩-⟨2,1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-3,3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩-⟨2,1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-3,2⟩\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (-3)+(-3)\cdot (-3)+3\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{3}^{2}}\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{19}\cdot \sqrt{22}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{418}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{12}{\sqrt{418}})≈{54}^{∘}.
$$

First, since $p\cdot q=-5$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =-5 \\ 4t\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 3+t\cdot (-3) & =-5 \\ 4t-6-3t & =-5 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨4(1),-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $p$ and $q$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{p\cdot q}{|\,p\,||\,q\,|} \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}+{p}_{z}{q}_{z}}{\sqrt{{p}_{x}^{2}+{p}_{y}^{2}+{p}_{z}^{2}}\sqrt{{q}_{x}^{2}+{q}_{y}^{2}+{q}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-5}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{\sqrt{21}\cdot \sqrt{19}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{\sqrt{399}}.\end{aligned}
$$

THerefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{399}})≈{104.5}^{∘}.
$$

after.problem: Consider the points $A(3t,t,4),$ $B(3t,4t,3)$ and $C(5t,t+1,5).$ Find $∠BAC$ given that $\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}=2.$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
after.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A,$ $B$ and $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨3t,\,t,\,4⟩,\,b=⟨3t,\,4t,\,3⟩,\,c=⟨5t,\,t+1,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠BAC=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13964292/assets/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨3t,\,4t,\,3⟩-⟨3t,\,t,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,3t,\,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨5t,\,t+1,\,5⟩-⟨3t,\,t,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}=2$, we can solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC} & =2 \\ 0\cdot 2t+3t\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 1 & =2 \\ 3t-1 & =2 \\ 3t & =3 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨0,3,-1⟩, \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =⟨2,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{10}\cdot \sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{2}{2\sqrt{15}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}})≈{75}^{∘}.
$$

after.problem: Consider the points $D(t,5,3)$, $E({t}^{2},2,t)$ and $F(t+3,{t}^{2},1).$ Find $∠EDF$ given that $\overset{\to }{DE}\cdot \overset{\to }{DF}=6.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
after.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $D$, $E$, $F$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}d=⟨t,\,5,\,3⟩,\,e=⟨{t}^{2},\,2,\,t⟩,\,f=⟨t+3,\,{t}^{2},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△DEF$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠EDF=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13964292/assets/c9cfb3e84e6f76d243125f2a09246b2a1300a0134e71359bb2b528082f064f93.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{DE}$ and $\overset{\to }{DF}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{DE} & =e-d \\  & =⟨{t}^{2},\,2,\,t⟩-⟨t,\,5,\,3⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-t,\,-3,\,t-3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{DF} & =f-d \\  & =⟨t+3,\,{t}^{2},\,1⟩-⟨t,\,5,\,3⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,{t}^{2}-5,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\overset{\to }{DE}\cdot \overset{\to }{DF}=6$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{DE}\cdot \overset{\to }{DF} & =6 \\ ({t}^{2}-t)\cdot 3+(-3)\cdot ({t}^{2}-5)+(t-3)\cdot (-2) & =6 \\ 3{t}^{2}-3t-3{t}^{2}+15-2t+6 & =6 \\ -5t+21 & =6 \\ -5t & =-15 \\ t & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{DE} & =⟨{3}^{2}-3,-3,3-3⟩ \\  & =⟨6,-3,0⟩, \\ \overset{\to }{DF} & =⟨3,{3}^{2}-5,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨3,4,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{DE}$ and $\overset{\to }{DF}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{DE}\cdot \overset{\to }{DF}}{|\overset{\to }{DE}||\overset{\to }{DF}|} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{6}{3\sqrt{5}\cdot \sqrt{29}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{145}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{2}{\sqrt{145}})≈{80.44}^{∘}.
$$

Note that the position vectors of the points D, E, F are

d=⟨t,5,3⟩,e=⟨t2,2,t⟩,f=⟨t+3,t2,1⟩.

The triangle △DEF is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote ∠EDF=θ.

First, we find the components of DE→ and DF→: DE→=e−d=⟨t2,2,t⟩−⟨t,5,3⟩=⟨t2−t,−3,t−3⟩DF→=f−d=⟨t+3,t2,1⟩−⟨t,5,3⟩=⟨3,t2−5,−2⟩

DE→⋅DF→=6(t2−t)⋅3+(−3)⋅(t2−5)+(t−3)⋅(−2)=63t2−3t−3t2+15−2t+6=6−5t+21=6−5t=−15t=3

Next, the cosine of the angle between DE→ and DF→ is

cos⁡θ=DE→⋅DF→|DE→||DF→|=662+(−3)2+0232+42+(−2)2=635⋅29=2145.

Therefore, θ=arccos⁡(2145)≈80.44∘.

after.problem: Consider the points $A(t,1,1)$, $B(3t,1,3)$ and $C(3,-2,{t}^{2}).$ Find $∠BAC$ given that $\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}=4.$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
after.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A$, $B$, $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨t,\,1,\,1⟩,\,b=⟨3t,\,1,\,3⟩,\,c=⟨3,\,-2,\,{t}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠BAC=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13964292/assets/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨3t,\,1,\,3⟩-⟨t,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,0,\,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,{t}^{2}⟩-⟨t,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨3-t,\,-3,\,{t}^{2}-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}=4$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC} & =4 \\ 2t\cdot (3-t)+0\cdot (-3)+2\cdot ({t}^{2}-1) & =4 \\ 6t-2{t}^{2}+0+2{t}^{2}-2 & =4 \\ 6t-2 & =4 \\ 6t & =6 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨2,0,2⟩, \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =⟨3-1,\,3,\,{1}^{2}-1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-3,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{8}\cdot \sqrt{13}} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{26}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{26}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{2}{\sqrt{26}})≈{67}^{∘}.
$$

a=⟨t,1,1⟩,b=⟨3t,1,3⟩,c=⟨3,−2,t2⟩.

So, AB→=⟨2,0,2⟩,AC→=⟨3−1,3,12−1⟩=⟨2,−3,0⟩.

Next, the cosine of the angle between AB→ and AC→ is

cos⁡θ=AB→⋅AC→|AB→||AC→|=422+02+2222+(−3)2+02=48⋅13=4226=226.

Therefore, θ=arccos⁡(226)≈67∘.
